newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish lower house seals lower tax, PM blasts vote.
newsitem.headline: Polish lower house seals lower tax, PM blasts vote.

text.p: Poland's lower house of parliament unexpectedly voted on Thursday to substantially cut personal tax levels next year and Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz said the decision would strike at public finances.

"This vote is a disgrace to the majority in parliament," Cimoszewicz angrily told the chamber after deputies approved a bill changing personal tax levels to 17, 20, 33, and 45 percent from the current 21, 33, and 45 percent.

Kolodko made clear the new tax level and the resulting revenue gap would hamper work on next year's budget, due to be submitted to parliament next week, because it would require either radical cuts in spending or an increase of budget deficit.

Earlier this week Wednesday, Kolodko on behalf of the government proposed a more modest cut of tax levels, to 20, 31 and 43 percent, but the motion was backed on Thursday only by Cimoszewicz's ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD), the coalition's stronger partner.

The Polish Peasant Party (PSL), a smaller group in the government, voted along with the opposition to reduce the lowest tax level to 17 percent, signalling another rift in the often-uneasy three-year-old coalition.
But the leaders of the SLD and Peasants, Jozef Oleksy and Waldemar Pawlak, told reporters after the vote that the coalition was not about to fall apart.

Cimoszewicz, clearly shaken, said the support for the 17-percent tax level was a political gesture by the Peasants and other parties, meant to boost their popularity ahead of next year's parliamentary elections.
Cimoszewicz said the PSL had reneged on a behind-the-scenes deal over the tax bill, clinched during his meeting with the party's leadership late on Wednesday.
He said the Peasants had agreed to back the government-sponsored tax levels in exchange for SLD support for a bill granting subsidies for fuel used by farmers.

"Yesterday, when we met with the PSL leadership, the situation was much simpler, arguments were simpler, subsidies for fuels for farmers in exchange for supporting the government motion," he told parliament.

Kolodko earlier said his proposal to cut tax levels to 20, 31 and 43 percent would require keeping the 1997 budget deficit at this year's level of 2.8 percent of gross domestic product, rather than cutting it to 2.6 percent as earlier planned.
The central bank said that even this small increase in the deficit could endanger Kolodko's goal of reducing year-on-year inflation to 13 percent in December next year from September's 19.5 percent.
